extracted.intended_audience: copyright practitioners, creators using generative AI, policymakers, and stakeholders concerned with authorship of AI-assisted works
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when works involving generative AI (or AI-assisted tools) qualify for copyright protection under U.S. law, focusing on human authorship, originality, prompts, and human contributions. Applies legal tests and illustrative case law to evaluate various kinds of human-AI contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality requirement (not sweat of the brow)
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality is required for copyright protection; mere time and effort ('sweat of the brow') are insufficient. The requisite level of creativity is extremely low; even a slight amount will suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Feist: ideas or facts are not protectible; must have some creative spark 'no matter how crude, humble or obvious.' Use this test when assessing whether human contributions reach the minimum creativity threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-authored contributions necessary for copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: Works created solely by nonhumans (e.g., animals, machines) generally are not copyrightable; humans involved in the creation process must contribute in a way that qualifies as authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites cases (e.g., Naruto/monkey; Thaler) and explains that human involvement can make a work copyrightable to the extent contributions qualify as authorship. Evaluate whether the human provided protectable expression rather than only ideas or facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-as-tool vs. stand-in distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a machine (including AI) as a tool does not negate copyright protection, but where the system makes expressive choices (acts as a stand-in for human creativity) further analysis is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine how the system is being used (the process/usage), not merely its technical characteristics. If AI merely assists/enhances human expression, protection is not necessarily limited; if AI makes the expressive choices, authorship is doubtful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient human-authored expressive elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A resulting work is copyrightable only if it contains sufficient human-authored expressive elements (i.e., human-originated expression that meets originality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Burrow-Giles: photographer's choices (posing, arranging, evoking expression) supported authorship. Evaluate concrete human expressive acts (selection, arrangement, expression) embedded in the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint authorship requires copyrightable contribution and intent to merge
rubrics_metrics.description: To be a joint author, each co-author must contribute a non-trivial amount of creative, original, or intellectual expression and intend that their contributions be merged into a unitary work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (Brownstein, Ashton-Tate, CCNV, Andrien) show that merely providing ideas, sketches, directions, or commissioning is insufficient. The contributor must translate idea into protectable expression and intend combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioning, suggestions, or ideas alone are not authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Commissioning a work or offering detailed suggestions/directions ordinarily constitutes unprotectible ideas and does not, by itself, create authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites CCNV and Andrien: commissioning and providing detailed suggestions/directions were insufficient; courts treat such contributions as unprotectible ideas unless the contributor actually creates the expression or the implementer performs only rote transcription.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorization to embody requires only mechanical transcription
rubrics_metrics.description: When one authorizes another to embody expression in a copy, that embodiment must be a rote or mechanical transcription that does not require intellectual modification for the authorizer to be credited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Andrien: authorization to embody must be 'rote or mechanical transcription' — if the implementing party materially changes substance, authorship resides with the creator of the tangible expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI cannot be a joint author; analogy to joint authorship for assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Because AI systems are not human beings, they cannot be 'authors' or joint authors, but joint-authorship principles are a useful analogy for assessing sufficiency of human contribution to AI-generated output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use joint-authorship tests to evaluate whether a human's contribution to an AI output is a copyrightable contribution (non-trivial, original, intended to be merged).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three types of human contribution to AI-generated outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Human contributions commonly fall into three categories: (1) prompts that instruct an AI system to generate an output; (2) expressive inputs that can be perceived in AI-generated outputs; and (3) modifications or arrangements of AI-generated outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess each type separately and in combination; many cases will involve multiple contribution types. Use category to guide authorship and originality analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt copyrightability is distinct from output copyrightability
rubrics_metrics.description: Prompts themselves, if sufficiently creative, may be copyrightable as expressions, but copyright in a prompt does not automatically give copyright in the AI-generated output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the textual prompt is protectable, the output must independently meet human-authorship/originality criteria to be copyrighted in the user's favor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple or generic prompts insufficient for authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Inputting simple, generic, or minimal prompts is generally insufficient to make a user the author of the AI-generated output; such prompts are often unprotectible ideas or instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many stakeholders (ASCAP, BLIP, UMG) argued that one- or two-word or general prompts are unlikely to satisfy minimum human-expression standards. Treat simple prompts as non-authorial absent significant additional human contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highly detailed or sophisticated prompts may suffice (rare)
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly detailed, iterative, and sophisticated prompts that specify details of an output—such that the model output reflects the user's original conception—may be sufficient to meet the human-authorship requirement in some cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some academics and commenters assert detailed prompts that control expressive elements (lighting, pose, style, etc.) can confer authorship; however, the Office notes this may be rare and context-dependent. Evidence of specificity and the output reflecting those specifics is key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative prompting and demonstrable human effort as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeatedly revising prompts and iterating many times (including hundreds of iterations) can demonstrate greater human control and significant human effort, potentially supporting an authorship claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider amount of iteration, demonstrable human decision-making in refining outputs, and whether iteration produced control over expressive elements. But iterative prompting may still be compared to roulette/spinning where unpredictability undermines authorship claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship-by-adoption theory is contested and limited
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that a user becomes an author by adopting an AI-produced output (i.e., selecting and accepting it) is contentious; adoption alone risks vesting rights in mere ideas and is viewed skeptically by many commentators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office highlights critiques: mere acceptance/selection without contributing protectable expression should not create authorship; courts caution against substituting post-execution adoption for authorial participation in giving physical form to a work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-translation reduces user's control claim
rubrics_metrics.description: When prompts are given in one medium (e.g., text) and the AI produces another medium (e.g., image, audio), the necessary interpretation by the AI reduces the user's direct control over execution and weakens claims of authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether cross-medium translation required substantive interpretive choices by the AI; where AI makes significant interpretive decisions, user control may be indirect and insufficient for authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black-box unpredictability undermines claim of control
rubrics_metrics.description: Because many generative AI systems are 'black boxes' whose internal workings and decision processes are not transparent or predictable, it is difficult to show that a prompt deterministically produced specific expressive elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider lack of predictability and explainability when assessing whether a user's prompts meaningfully controlled the expressive outcome; inability to explain why certain elements appeared is evidence against authorial control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of possible outputs limits copyright in prompts' scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the same prompt can generate a multiplicity of distinct outputs, extending copyright protection in a written prompt to cover all potential outputs risks effectively conferring a copyright in a method/process, which is excluded under 17 U.S.C. § 102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating prompts as conferring broad proprietary rights over a generative method; assess copyright narrowly to protect expression but not ideas/methods/processes.
